MATH3603 Deep Learning & Explainable AI ─ Assignment 1¶

This assignment is designed to test your basic understanding of artificial neural networks. The task consists of two parts with practical questions for you to answer using Python:

Part A. Define and implement the basic elements of a neural network [40 marks]
Part B. Carry out image classification using a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) [60 marks]

The maximum number of marks for each part is shown above, with a total of 100 marks available. Partial marks for individual tasks are shown below in the section headings.

This is a summative assessment contributing 30% to the final module grade.

Objectives¶

Through this assignment you will:

  • Demonstrate understanding of the design and essential ingredients of a simple neural network.
  • Design and build your first deep neural network (DNN).
  • Train a DNN model for image classification of natural scene data.
  • Use various metrics to ascertain how your DNN model is performing.

Setup and resources¶

  • You must work using the template notebook provided with the task.
  • Please do not remove anything in the template. You are allowed to add new code cells.
  • You should implement this assignment using Python and PyTorch.

Having a GPU will speed up the training process. See the document "Computing Information Sheet" on Minerva about setting up a working environment and various ways to access a GPU.

Required packages¶

Please make sure that you have the following basic packages installed before you begin:

  • numpy is a package for scientific computing with Python
  • h5py is a package to interact with compactly stored datasets
  • matplotlib can be used for plotting graphs in Python
  • PyTorch is a library widely used for building deep-learning frameworks

If needed, you can install these and other packages using pip or conda.

Importing some other packages may be required; hints are provided for you in the template below.

Submission¶

Due date¶

The assignment is released on Minerva on Friday 9th October 2026 and is due for submission via Gradescope by 09:00 on Monday 2nd November 2026.

If you submit your work past the deadline, penalties will be applied: for every period of 24 hours or part thereof that your assessment is overdue, you will lose 5% of the total marks available for that assessment component. This includes weekends, Bank Holidays and University closed days.

If you are unable to submit your work on time, please consider applying for an extension or exemption due to mitigating circumstances.

What to submit¶

Please submit a single *.zip file through Minerva Gradebook Submission, comprising the following files:

  1. Your completed Jupyter notebook as *.ipynb file.
  2. The *.html version of your notebook (saved using File > Save and Export Notebook As > HTML).
  3. Academic integrity statement (signed and dated) including the Gen AI use disclosure.

Further guidance¶

  • In each section, put the relevant code containing your solution.
  • When defining a function, please add a description of the arguments, along with their dimensions (shapes).
  • Please annotate your code as appropriate to make it more readable for humans and to explain your chain of thought.
  • You may re-use functions you defined previously, but any new code must be in the relevant section.
  • Feel free to add as many code cells as you need under each section.
  • Before submission, check that all Python cells have been run.
  • Make sure that all outputs (including all graphs you would like to be marked) are displayed in the *.html file that you will submit for marking.

Part A: Design and Ingredients of a Neural Network [40 marks]¶

Tasks¶

A1. Define the sigmoid activation function and plot its graph [10 marks]
A2. Implement forward pass including weights [10 marks]
A3. Define and evaluate the cost value [10 marks]
A4. Implement backward pass and update the weights [10 marks]

To answer these questions, please provide the required Python code in the code cells below and run it on a specific DNN example shown below:


This figure represents a two-layer neural network (with sigmoid activation functions) for classification of 2D input vectors $\begin{bmatrix}x_1\\x_2\end{bmatrix}$ into 2 x 2 = 4 classes labelled $\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix}$, $\begin{bmatrix}1\\0\end{bmatrix}$, $\begin{bmatrix}0\\1\end{bmatrix}$, and $\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}$. The input values, as well as the associated weights and biases in each layer, are shown in the figure. The neurons in the output layer produce their scalar predictions independently, with the corresponding ground truth 0/1 shown on the right.


Notation:

$x$ -- training instance (input)
$y_{\text{true}}$ -- ground truth
$z$ -- affine transformation of $x$
$w$ -- weight
$b$ -- bias
$a$ -- activation through sigmoid

In [2]:
import numpy as np 
#Useful package for working with vectors/matrices

A1. Activation function [10 marks]¶

A1.1. Define the sigmoid activation function¶

The sigmoid sfunction is defined as:

$$\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$$

Its range is the interval $(0, 1)$ with large values mapping close to 1 and small (i.e increasingly negative) values mapping close to 0 (Note: $\sigma(0) = 0.5$)

In [3]:
# Your code here:
def sigmoid(x):
    '''
    Arguments:
        x: scalar or n-dimensional array, shape(n, )
    Returns: 
        sigmoid(x) for all (or just one) elements in x
    '''
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-x))

A1.2. Print sigmoid(-0.2) = <value> with 4 decimal places¶

In [4]:
# Your code here:
print(f'sigmoid(-0.2) = {round(sigmoid(-0.2), 4)}')

sigmoid(-0.2) = 0.4502

A1.3. Plot the graph of y = sigmoid(x)¶

In [5]:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

xmin, xmax, n = -8, 8, 100

#Generates n evenly spaced points in the interval [xmin, xmax]
x = np.linspace(xmin, xmax, n)

#Compute sigmoid(x) for each element in x
y = sigmoid(x)

#Some prettying up of the plot
plt.xlabel('x')
plt.ylabel('y')
plt.title('Sigmoid activation function')
plt.grid(alpha=0.3)

#Horizontal asymptotes
plt.axhline(0, color="grey", ls="--", lw=0.8)
plt.axhline(1, color="grey", ls="--", lw=0.8)


#Plotting
plt.plot(x, y, label=r"$\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$")
plt.legend(loc='upper left')
plt.show()

A2. Forward propagation [10 marks]¶

A2.1. Define forward pass¶

In [6]:
def forward_pass(W, b, X):
    """  
    Feeding-forward of inputs through the network
    Arguments:
        W: Array of network weights, shape (p, n)
        b: Array of network biases, shape (p, )
        X: input vector, shape (n, )

    Returns:
        Z: array of affine outputs
        A: array of sigmoid-transformed outputs
    """

# Forward propagation (affine transform)
#Initialise the arrays storing the outputs
    Z, A = [], []
    #Output from previous layer, start with inital input vector
    a_prev = X
    
# Activation
    for W_l, b_l in zip(W, b):
        z = np.matmul(W_l, a_prev) + b_l
        a = sigmoid(z)
        Z.append(z)
        A.append(a)
        
        #Reset a_prev to new value so loop can start for next layer
        a_prev = a

    return Z, A

A2.2. Find forward pass for the hidden layer¶

In [7]:
# Your code here:
X = np.array([0.1, 0.5])

W = np.array([
    #Layer 1
    [[0.1, 0.3],
     [0.2, 0.4]],
    
    #Layer 2
     [[0.5, 0.6],
      [0.7, 0.8]]
])

b = np.array([
    
    [0.25, 0.25], #Layer 1
    [0.35, 0.35]  #Layer 2
])

Z, A = forward_pass(W, b, X)

#index n=0 is the forward pass for first hidden layer
#with indexes n=n+1 being forward passes for successive hidden 
#layers and index -1 (last index) being output. In this case,
#only one hidden layer

print(f'Z for hidden layer: {Z[0]}')
print(f'A for hidden layer: {A[0]}')

Z for hidden layer: [0.41 0.47]
A for hidden layer: [0.60108788 0.61538376]
In [8]:
# Optional: manual check

# print(W.T)

# print(W[0])

#Matrix multiplication gives result from feedforward of 
#inputs through first hidden layer
Z_11, Z_12 = np.matmul(W[0], X) + b[0]


print(Z_11)
print(Z_12)


print(sigmoid(Z_11), sigmoid(Z_12))

Outputs from neurones can be thought of as probability that (the network 'thinks') the correct label is 1

A3. Cost value [10 marks]¶

A3.1. Define the cost using negative log-liklihood loss (binary cross entropy)¶

In [10]:
def cost(Y_out, Y_true):
    """
    negative log-likelihood cost function`, averaged over the output neurons.
    
    Arguments:
        Y_out: predicted probabilities of label 1 (output of the sigmoid), shape (n,)
        Y_true: ground-truth labels, each 0 or 1, shape (n,)

    Returns:
        J: scalar cost
    """
    
    # Your code here
    # probability the network gave to the true label: y_hat if y = 1, (1 - y_hat) if y = 0
    p_true = Y_true * Y_out + (1 - Y_true) * (1 - Y_out)
    return -np.mean(np.log(p_true))

A3.2. Find the cost over one iteration (forward pass)¶

In [11]:

y_true = np.array([0, 1])

cost1 = cost(output, y_true)

print(f'Cost: \n{cost1}')

A4. Backward propagation [10 marks]¶

This is the process of changing the DNN parameters (weights/biases) using the gradient descent algorithm (at a certain learning rate).

A4.1. Define backward pass¶

In [12]:
#Sigmoid function derivative can be nicely written in terms
#of the original function

def sigmoid_derivative(x):
    return sigmoid(x) * (1 - sigmoid(x))

def backward_pass(W, b, X, Z, A, Y_true):
    """
    Backward propagation (chain rule) for the network
    Computes gradients using the current weights.

    Arguments:
        W: array of weight matrices, shape (p, n)
        b: array of bias vectors, each (p,)
        X: input vector, shape (n,)
        Z: array of affine outputs from forward_pass
        A: array of activations from forward_pass
        Y_true: ground-truth labels

    Returns:
        dW: list of gradients dJ/dW[l], same shapes as W
        db: list of gradients dJ/db[l], same shapes as b
        cost_value: cost for this forward pass
    """
    N = len(Y_true)
    y_hat = A[-1]

    #output layer
    dA2 = (-(Y_true / y_hat) + (1 - Y_true) / (1 - y_hat)) / N   # dJ/da^[2]            
    dZ2 = dA2 * sigmoid_derivative(Z[1])                         # dJ/dz^[2]           
    dW2 = np.outer(dZ2, A[0])                                    # dJ/dW^[2] = dz2 a1^T 
    db2 = dZ2                                                    # dJ/db^[2]            

    #hidden layer (error sent back through the OLD output weights)
    dA1 = np.matmul(W[1].T, dZ2)                                 # dJ/da^[1]          
    dZ1 = dA1 * sigmoid_derivative(Z[0])                         # dJ/dz^[1]            
    dW1 = np.outer(dZ1, X)                                       # dJ/dW^[1] = dz1 x^T  
    db1 = dZ1                                                    # dJ/db^[1]            

    # Return gradients (of weights and biases seperately), and cost
    return [dW1, dW2], [db1, db2], cost(y_hat, Y_true)

A4.2. Implement backward pass and update the output layer¶

In [13]:
# Your code here


Y_true = np.array([0, 1])
learning_rate = 0.1  # eta (step size of gradient descent)

dW, db, J = backward_pass(W, b, X, Z, A, Y_true)
print(f"Cost before update: {J:.4f}\n")
print("dJ/dW^[2] =\n", dW[1])
print("dJ/db^[2] =", db[1])

# Work on copies so the original parameters stay available for comparison
W_new = [w.copy() for w in W]
b_new = [v.copy() for v in b]

# Gradient-descent update of the output layer
W_new[1] = W[1] - learning_rate * dW[1]
b_new[1] = b[1] - learning_rate * db[1]

print("\nUpdated W^[2] =\n", W_new[1])
print("Updated b^[2] =", b_new[1])

Dataset¶

This assignment will use a subset of images from the Tiny ImageNet dataset. This subset contains 30 different categories and will be referred to as TinyImageNet30. The training set has 450 resized images (64 x 64 pixels) for each category (13,500 images in total). You can download the training and test sets from Kaggle or directly from here:

One challenge of building a deep learning model is to choose an architecture that can learn the features in the dataset without being unnecessarily complex. The first part of the assignment involves building an MLP (type of DNN) and training it on TinyImageNet30.

B1. Image classification: overview and implementation [20 marks]¶

B1.1. PyTorch data classes¶

Write PyTorch classes Dataset to load the TinyImage30 dataset and DataLoaders to create training and validation subsets.

In [19]:
# Your code here:
import os

from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

# ---------- settings ----------
data_dir = "Assessment_1_data/train_set/train_set"   
image_size = 64                     # images are 64 x 64 pixels
SEED = 0                            # seed for reproducibility
test_ratio = 0.2                    # fraction of the data used for validation
batch_size = 128

# Use a GPU when available
device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available()
                      else "mps" if torch.backends.mps.is_available() else "cpu")
print("Using device:", device)

def set_seed(seed):
    """Make python / numpy / torch random numbers reproducible."""
    import random
    random.seed(seed)
    np.random.seed(seed)
    torch.manual_seed(seed)
    torch.cuda.manual_seed_all(seed)

set_seed(SEED)


class TinyImageNet30(Dataset):
    """
    Loads TinyImageNet30 data.

    All images are read once and kept in memory as a  tensor then
    they are converted to normalised floats

    Arguments:
        root: path to the folder that contains one sub-folder per class
        image_size: images are resized to (image_size, image_size) if they are not already

    Attributes:
        images: uint8 tensor, shape (N, 3, image_size, image_size)
        labels: long tensor,  shape (N,), class index of each image
        classes: list of class names (sorted folder names); index in the list = label
    """

    def __init__(self, root, image_size=64):
        self.classes = sorted(d for d in os.listdir(root)
                              if os.path.isdir(os.path.join(root, d)))
        self.class_to_idx = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(self.classes)}

        images, labels = [], []
        for c in self.classes:
            folder = os.path.join(root, c)
            for fname in sorted(os.listdir(folder)):
                if not fname.lower().endswith((".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png")):
                    continue                                    # ignore non-image files
                img = Image.open(os.path.join(folder, fname)).convert("RGB")   # force 3 channels
                if img.size != (image_size, image_size):
                    img = img.resize((image_size, image_size))
                images.append(np.asarray(img, dtype=np.uint8))  # (H, W, 3)
                labels.append(self.class_to_idx[c])

        # (N, H, W, 3) -> (N, 3, H, W) as PyTorch expects channels first
        self.images = torch.from_numpy(np.stack(images)).permute(0, 3, 1, 2).contiguous()
        self.labels = torch.tensor(labels, dtype=torch.long)

        # per-channel mean / std used for normalisation (set later from the training split only)
        self.mean = torch.zeros(3, 1, 1)
        self.std = torch.ones(3, 1, 1)

    def set_normalisation(self, mean, std):
        self.mean = mean.view(3, 1, 1)
        self.std = std.view(3, 1, 1)

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.labels)

    def __getitem__(self, idx):
        x = self.images[idx].float() / 255.0          # scale pixels to [0, 1]
        x = (x - self.mean) / self.std                # standardise each colour channel
        return x, self.labels[idx]


class SubsetDataset(Dataset):
    """
    A view on part of a dataset (given by `indices`) with optional data augmentation.
    Augmentation = random horizontal flip with probability 0.5 (training split only).
    """

    def __init__(self, dataset, indices, augment=False):
        self.dataset, self.indices, self.augment = dataset, indices, augment

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.indices)

    def __getitem__(self, i):
        x, y = self.dataset[self.indices[i]]
        if self.augment and torch.rand(1).item() < 0.5:
            x = torch.flip(x, dims=[2])               # flip along the width axis
        return x, y

# Your code here to define the MLP Model
class MLP(nn.Module):
    """
    Fully connected network (multilayer perceptron) for image classification.

    Arguments:
        input_dim: number of input units = 3 * 64 * 64 = 12288 (flattened RGB image)
        hidden_dims: tuple with the number of hidden units of each hidden layer
        num_classes: number of output units (one per class) = 30
        dropout: probability of zeroing a hidden unit during training (regularisation)

    Inputs:  
        x of shape (batch, 3, 64, 64)
    Outputs: 
        logits of shape (batch, num_classes)   (softmax is applied inside the loss)
    """

    def __init__(self, input_dim=3 * image_size * image_size, hidden_dims=(512, 256),
                 num_classes=30, dropout=0.3):
        super().__init__()
        layers = [nn.Flatten()]                       # (batch, 3, 64, 64) -> (batch, 12288)
        prev = input_dim
        for h in hidden_dims:
            layers += [nn.Linear(prev, h),            # affine transformation
                       nn.ReLU(),                     # non-linear activation
                       nn.Dropout(dropout)]           # regularisation
            prev = h
        layers.append(nn.Linear(prev, num_classes))   # output layer: one logit per class
        self.net = nn.Sequential(*layers)

        for m in self.modules():                      # He initialisation suits ReLU units
            if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
                nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)

    def forward(self, x):
        return self.net(x)


def count_parameters(model):
    """Number of trainable parameters."""
    return sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters() if p.requires_grad)


def make_training_objects(model, lr=5e-4, weight_decay=1e-4):
    """Loss function and optimiser used to train the model."""
    criterion = nn.CrossEntropyLoss()                 # softmax + negative log-likelihood for 30 classes
    optimiser = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr, weight_decay=weight_decay)
    return criterion, optimiser


set_seed(SEED)
model = MLP(num_classes=num_classes).to(device)
print(model)
print(f"\nTrainable parameters: {count_parameters(model):,}")

# (HelperDL function) -- Define top-*k* accuracy
def topk_accuracy(output, target, topk=(1,)):
    """
    Computes Precision@k for the specified range of top images returned by the model.
    This evaluation metric measures the proportion of relevant results out of top k. 
    
    """
    
    maxk = max(topk)
    batch_size = target.size(0)
    _, pred = output.topk(maxk, 1, True, True)
    pred = pred.t()
    correct = pred.eq(target.view(1, -1).expand_as(pred))

    res = []
    for k in topk:
        correct_k = correct[:k].view(-1).float().sum(0)
        res.append(correct_k.mul_(100.0 / batch_size))
    return res

# Your code --> Running your MLP model class
import copy
import time

def topk_accuracy_safe(output, target, topk=(1,)):
    """
    Same as the provided topk_accuracy, but uses .reshape(-1) instead of .view(-1).
    With recent PyTorch versions the provided helper raises
    "RuntimeError: view size is not compatible with input tensor's size and stride"
    because `correct[:k]` is a non-contiguous slice of a transposed tensor.
    """
    maxk = max(topk)
    batch_size = target.size(0)
    _, pred = output.topk(maxk, 1, True, True)        # indices of the maxk highest scores
    pred = pred.t()
    correct = pred.eq(target.view(1, -1).expand_as(pred))
    return [correct[:k].reshape(-1).float().sum(0) * (100.0 / batch_size) for k in topk]

def run_epoch(model, loader, criterion, optimiser=None):
    """
    One pass over `loader`. Trains the model if an optimiser is given, otherwise only evaluates.

    Returns:
        average loss, top-1 accuracy (%), top-5 accuracy (%) over the whole loader
    """
    training = optimiser is not None
    model.train(training)                             # enables / disables dropout
    total_loss = top1 = top5 = 0.0
    n = 0
    with torch.set_grad_enabled(training):            # no gradients needed for evaluation
        for x, y in loader:
            x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device)
            out = model(x)                            # forward pass -> logits (batch, 30)
            loss = criterion(out, y)
            if training:
                optimiser.zero_grad()
                loss.backward()                       # backward pass
                optimiser.step()                      # gradient-descent style update
            bs = y.size(0)
            a1, a5 = topk_accuracy_safe(out, y, topk=(1, 5))
            total_loss += loss.item() * bs
            top1 += a1.item() * bs
            top5 += a5.item() * bs
            n += bs
    return total_loss / n, top1 / n, top5 / n


max_epochs = 60          # upper limit on the number of epochs
patience = 10            # stop if validation loss has not improved for this many epochs

set_seed(SEED)
model = MLP(num_classes=num_classes).to(device)
criterion, optimiser = make_training_objects(model)

history = {"train_loss": [], "val_loss": [], "train_acc": [], "val_acc": [], "val_top5": []}
best_val_loss, best_epoch, best_state, epochs_without_improvement = float("inf"), 0, None, 0

start = time.time()
for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
    tr_loss, tr_acc, _ = run_epoch(model, train_loader, criterion, optimiser)
    va_loss, va_acc, va_top5 = run_epoch(model, val_loader, criterion)

    history["train_loss"].append(tr_loss); history["val_loss"].append(va_loss)
    history["train_acc"].append(tr_acc);   history["val_acc"].append(va_acc)
    history["val_top5"].append(va_top5)

    print(f"Epoch {epoch:3d} | train loss {tr_loss:.4f} acc {tr_acc:5.2f}% | "
          f"val loss {va_loss:.4f} acc {va_acc:5.2f}% (top-5 {va_top5:5.2f}%)")

    if va_loss < best_val_loss:                       # keep the weights with the lowest validation loss
        best_val_loss, best_epoch = va_loss, epoch
        best_state = copy.deepcopy(model.state_dict())
        epochs_without_improvement = 0
    else:
        epochs_without_improvement += 1
        if epochs_without_improvement >= patience:    # early stopping
            print(f"Early stopping: no improvement for {patience} epochs.")
            break

# Your code here
@torch.no_grad()
def get_predictions(model, loader):
    """
    Run the model over a whole loader.

    Returns:
        probs  -- np.ndarray (N, num_classes), softmax probabilities
        labels -- np.ndarray (N,), true class indices
    """
    model.eval()
    probs, labels = [], []
    for x, y in loader:
        out = model(x.to(device))
        probs.append(torch.softmax(out, dim=1).cpu())
        labels.append(y)
    return torch.cat(probs).numpy(), torch.cat(labels).numpy()


def confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred, num_classes):
    """cm[i, j] = number of samples of true class i predicted as class j."""
    cm = np.zeros((num_classes, num_classes), dtype=np.int64)
    np.add.at(cm, (y_true, y_pred), 1)
    return cm


def plot_confusion_matrix(cm, title):
    """
    Heat map in which each cell shows the PERCENTAGE OF THE WHOLE DATASET (100 * cm / total)
    having that (true class, predicted class) combination. The diagonal is the correctly classified data.
    """
    pct = 100.0 * cm / cm.sum()
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(14, 12))
    im = ax.imshow(pct, cmap="Blues")
    for i in range(cm.shape[0]):
        for j in range(cm.shape[1]):
            if pct[i, j] >= 0.05:                         # hide 0.0 entries to keep the plot readable
                ax.text(j, i, f"{pct[i, j]:.1f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=6,
                        color="white" if pct[i, j] > 0.6 * pct.max() else "black")
    ax.set_xticks(range(cm.shape[1])); ax.set_yticks(range(cm.shape[0]))
    ax.set_xticklabels(range(cm.shape[1]), fontsize=7); ax.set_yticklabels(range(cm.shape[0]), fontsize=7)
    ax.set_xlabel("Predicted class"); ax.set_ylabel("True class")
    ax.set_title(f"{title}  (cell = % of all {cm.sum()} images; accuracy = {100 * np.trace(cm) / cm.sum():.1f}%)")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046, pad=0.04, label="% of dataset")
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.show()

# Your code here
def roc_curve_ovr(scores, is_positive):
    """
    One-vs-rest ROC curve for one class.

    Arguments:
        scores      -- (N,) predicted probability of this class
        is_positive -- (N,) boolean, True where the true label is this class

    Returns:
        fpr, tpr -- false / true positive rates over all decision thresholds, auc -- area under the curve
    """
    order = np.argsort(-scores)                       # lower the threshold from high to low scores
    s, pos = scores[order], is_positive[order]
    tps = np.cumsum(pos)                              # true positives at each threshold
    fps = np.cumsum(~pos)                             # false positives at each threshold
    last_of_ties = np.r_[np.where(np.diff(s))[0], len(s) - 1]   # one point per distinct threshold
    tpr = np.r_[0.0, tps[last_of_ties] / pos.sum()]
    fpr = np.r_[0.0, fps[last_of_ties] / (~pos).sum()]
    auc = np.sum(np.diff(fpr) * (tpr[1:] + tpr[:-1]) / 2)       # trapezoidal rule
    return fpr, tpr, auc


# per-class recall (diagonal / row sum of the validation confusion matrix) decides best / worst classes
val_recall = np.diag(cm_val) / cm_val.sum(axis=1)
val_auc = np.array([roc_curve_ovr(val_probs[:, k], val_labels == k)[2] for k in range(num_classes)])

ranking = np.argsort(-val_recall)
selected = list(ranking[:2]) + list(ranking[-2:])         # 2 highest then 2 lowest performing classes

print("Per-class validation results (sorted by recall):")
print(f"{'class idx':>9} {'name':>12} {'recall %':>9} {'AUC':>6}")
for k in ranking:
    tag = "  <- selected" if k in selected else ""
    print(f"{k:9d} {full_dataset.classes[k]:>12} {100 * val_recall[k]:9.1f} {val_auc[k]:6.3f}{tag}")
print(f"\nMacro-average one-vs-rest AUC (validation): {val_auc.mean():.3f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5.5), sharey=True)
for ax, (probs, labels, name) in zip(axes, [(val_probs, val_labels, "Validation set"),
                                            (train_probs, train_labels, "Training set")]):
    for rank, k in enumerate(selected):
        fpr, tpr, auc = roc_curve_ovr(probs[:, k], labels == k)
        kind = "best" if rank < 2 else "worst"
        ax.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"class {k} ({kind}), AUC = {auc:.3f}")
    ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", lw=0.8, label="chance (AUC = 0.5)")
    ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate"); ax.set_title(f"ROC curves - {name}")
    ax.grid(alpha=0.3); ax.legend(loc="lower right")
axes[0].set_ylabel("True positive rate")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
